analysis.one_liner: Bans abusive credit card fees and practices, requires clearer payoff disclosures, and restricts cards for minors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee at the end of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Credit CARD Act of 2007 would have restricted common credit card practices: card issuers would need to warn you 15 days before raising your interest rate and could not apply the increase to your existing balance, and they could not charge fees for paying on time, paying in full, or not using your card. It would also ban raising your rate because of unrelated late payments elsewhere ('universal default'), require statements to show how long and how much it takes to pay off your balance, and bar most credit cards for people under 18 unless a parent co-signs or the teen qualifies independently. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly four in five American households that carry credit card debt, especially people who pay late occasionally or carry a balance: they would have gotten warning before rate hikes, protection from retroactive increases on existing balances, freedom from fees for paying on time or not using the card, and statements that plainly show the true cost of minimum payments. Young consumers would have been shielded from pre-approved cards marketed on campuses.

how_it_helps.text: Requires at least 15 days' advance notice before an interest rate increase takes effect, and bars the new rate from applying to the balance you already owe. If you cancel the card instead, your old rate is frozen on the existing balance.

Bans several fee practices: charging interest on amounts paid on time and in full, fees for paying off your balance early, fees for not using your card, and over-the-limit fees on transactions the card issuer itself approved.
Prohibits 'universal default' — raising your card's interest rate because of late payments or credit problems unrelated to that card.

Requires monthly statements to show, prominently and in a table, how long it would take to pay off the balance with minimum payments and what monthly payment would clear the debt in 36 months, plus clear disclosure of late-payment deadlines and any penalty interest rate.

Bars most credit cards to people under 18 unless a parent or guardian signs on, the young person shows independent income, or they complete a credit counseling course, and applies the same rules to school-affiliated 'affinity' cards marketed to students.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and card companies whose revenue comes substantially from penalty interest rates, universal default, over-the-limit and inactivity fees, and interest charged on balances before payments are applied. They would lose those revenue streams and face doubled civil penalties for disclosure violations. Some borrowers with worsening overall finances would no longer face rate hikes tied to outside information, a cost issuers said would be spread across all cardholders through somewhat higher rates.

drawbacks.text: Banning the use of outside credit information to raise rates (a ban on 'universal default') removes one way issuers price for risk. Issuers argued restrictions like this mean higher interest rates across the board and tighter credit, because lenders can no longer reprice cards when a borrower's overall finances deteriorate. The bill does preserve index-based rate changes and lets issuers act on problems directly tied to the cardholder's own account [S3].

The advance-notice provision lets a cardholder cancel the account rather than accept a rate increase, keeping the old rate on the balance. Issuers could respond by being quicker to close accounts, which can temporarily dent a cardholder's credit score — a cost of the protection the bill itself acknowledges by design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the protections outweigh the costs: penalty fees and surprise rate hikes hit hardest the people who can least afford them, and the disclosure requirements simply tell borrowers the truth about their debts before they fall behind [S2][S3]. The good-faith objection is real, though: issuers price for risk, and barring them from raising rates when a borrower's outside finances deteriorate can mean higher rates for everyone and less credit for the shakiest borrowers; the bill partly softens this by allowing index-based rate adjustments and letting cardholders cancel before a rate increase takes effect [S3]. On balance this is a broadly pro-borrower bill with a genuine, but secondary, cost in credit availability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee after being referred there, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2007 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The full action history shows only introduction, sponsor remarks, and the committee referral — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the two-year Congress.
It drew 40 cosponsors, all House Democrats, indicating support among members that never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers were better off in the near term, because they kept charging penalty fees and raising rates through universal default. Cardholders benefited only later: a substantially similar Credit CARD Act became federal law in 2009, two years after this bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers, for two more years

for.name: Rep. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 9, 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver
for.what_they_did: Joined Udall as the bill's co-lead at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee Chairman Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote in the two years it sat before his committee.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on penalty rates, universal default, and card fees, arguing they would raise costs and restrict credit; the bill never advanced past referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors, plus the sponsor and co-lead, were House Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the bill died in committee under a Democratic committee chair.

industries.note: The bill bans several of the industry's most profitable practices — universal default, over-the-limit and inactivity fees, and surprise retroactive rate increases — and forces clearer payoff disclosures. It also tightens civil penalties for violating disclosure rules. Its core business of charging consumers penalty rates on existing balances at short notice would shrink.

The bill requires young applicants without a co-signer or income to complete counseling from a Board-approved nonprofit agency, which could channel new business to compliant agencies — but only those meeting strict conflict-of-interest and fee standards. Many agencies would fail the test.
